The reference is the APPROVED STYLE AND CONTINUITY anchor, not a sheet to copy unchanged. Not glossy coins or flat generic pictograms. Each icon is a complete perfect CIRCLE with opaque painted interior and transparent empty space outside. Center each circle in its own equal grid cell, circle diameter 80 percent of the shorter cell side, generous empty gutters. Absolutely no letters, names, numbers, grid lines, labels, UI, watermark or cast shadows outside circles. No modern laboratory hardware, books, houses or buildings. Only the specified object inside each circle, with a simple dark ground or essential local context. Tiny details must not carry the meaning. Related states should differ in structure, not merely colour. Follow item order exactly, left to right, top to bottom. Exactly 20 circles in 5 columns and 4 rows. Landscape atlas. Exact cell subjects: CELL 1, Roots: One sturdy green stem ends in a spreading fan of pale branching roots, revealed in a dark soil cutaway with fine rootlets reaching toward water pockets. CELL 3, Fallen wood: One thick broken dark branch lies diagonally, its pale torn end and a few attached bark strips clearly visible against a small patch of leaf litter. Distinguish: Single intact dead branch, without landscape devastation, fungal breakdown or sheltering animals. CELL 4, Fungi: A small group of ochre and ivory mushrooms grows from a dark fallen branch, with pale threadlike mycelium exposed beneath one lifted bark edge. CELL 5, Decomposition: A broken log crumbles into dark fibrous fragments beneath pale fungal threads and two small mushroom caps; the intact end transitions visibly into loose organic matter. Distinguish: Active material breakdown across the log, not fungi alone or already released nutrients entering roots. CELL 6, Returned nutrients: Small ochre and pale mineral flecks emerge from dark decomposed leaf fragments and gather beside fine roots in moist soil, following a short pale flow through the cutaway. Distinguish: Nutrient return into root-bearing soil, not simply a soil sample, intact decaying log or riverborne minerals. CELL 7, Renewing forest: A young green tree grows immediately beside an old dark stump, its roots visibly reaching through rich soil beneath a decaying branch; older trunks form a restrained background. Distinguish: New growth tied to ordinary ongoing decay in an established forest, without disaster damage or open horizon expansion. CELL 8, Peat: A cutaway of saturated dark brown ground exposes thick soft layers of recognizable pressed stems and leaves beneath a shallow mossy pool. Distinguish: Wet partly decomposed plant fibers remain visible, unlike crumbly topsoil, deep carbon seam or mineral sand. CELL 9, Buried carbon: A deep dark carbon-rich layer containing faint compressed plant traces lies beneath several thick ochre sediment beds and far below a small green surface. Distinguish: Deep burial and a distinct dark organic seam; not exposed wet peat or repeated alternating iron bands. CELL 10, Forest rain: A broad jade canopy sends fine pale moisture strokes upward into a low cloud that releases rain over the far edge of the same forest. Distinguish: Tree-to-cloud moisture connection dominates, rather than an ordinary shower or full sea-land water cycle. CELL 11, Arthropods: A dark ochre many-segmented shoreline animal has a clear external armored back, antennae and several pairs of visibly jointed legs.
